questions.q: Draw the circuit diagram of a Wheatstone bridge. Obtain the condition when no current flows through the galvanometer in it.
questions.solution:
By applying Kirchoff's loop rule to closed loops ADBA and CBDC
$-\mathrm{I}_1 \mathrm{R}_1+0+\mathrm{I}_2 \mathrm{R}_2=0$
-----(i) $\left[\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{g}}=0\right]$
$\mathrm{I}_2 \mathrm{R}_4+0-\mathrm{I}_1 \mathrm{R}_3=0$ ...(ii)
From eq (i)-
$\frac{I_1}{I_2}=\frac{R_2}{R_1}$
From eq (ii)-
$\frac{I_1}{I_2}=\frac{R_4}{R_3}$
Hence,
$\frac{R_2}{R_1}=\frac{R_4}{R_3}$

questions.q: Define the term 'mobility' of charge carriers in a current carrying conductor. Obtain the relation for mobility in terms of relaxation time.
questions.solution:
Mobility is defined as the magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric field.
$\mu=\frac{\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}}\right|}{\mathrm{E}}$
[Even if a student writes only the mathematical relation award $1 / 2$ mark]
Given $V_d=\frac{e \tau E}{m}$
Hence, $\mu=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}}{\mathrm{E}}=\frac{\mathrm{e} \tau}{\mathrm{m}}$
questions.subject: Physics

questions.q: Define the term 'drift velocity' of electrons in a current carrying conductor. Obtain the relationship between the current density and the drift velocity of electrons.
questions.solution:
The average speed with which electrons move when an electric field or potential difference is applied is called drift velocity.
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}}=\frac{-\mathrm{e} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \tau}{\mathrm{~m}}$
[Award $1 / 2$ mark if student writes the formulae]

The amount of charge crossing the area A in time $\Delta t$
$\mathrm{I} \Delta \mathrm{t}=\mathrm{ne} \mathrm{~A}\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{d}}}\right| \Delta \mathrm{t}$
Hence current density
$j=\frac{I}{A}=n e V_d$

questions.q: A 10 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected in parallel across a battery of emf 200 V and internal resistance $38 \Omega$ as shown in the figure. Find the value of current in the circuit.
questions.solution:
By Kirchoff's law, we have, for the loop ABCD , $+200-38 \mathrm{i}-10=0$
$\therefore i=\frac{190}{38} \mathrm{~A}=5 \mathrm{~A}$

Alternatively:
The two cells being in 'opposition', $\therefore$ net $\varepsilon \mathrm{mf}=(200-10) \mathrm{V}=190 \mathrm{~V}$
Now $I=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{R}$
$\therefore I=\frac{190 \mathrm{~V}}{38 \Omega}=5 \mathrm{~A}$
[Note: Some students may use the formulae $\frac{\varepsilon}{r}=\frac{\varepsilon_1}{r_1}+\frac{\varepsilon_2}{r_2}$, and
$r=\left(r_1 r_2\right) /\left(r_1+r_2\right)$
For two cells connected in parallel
They may then say that $\mathrm{r}=0$;
$\varepsilon$ is indeterminate and hence
I is also indeterminate
Award full marks(2) to students giving this line of reasoning.]

(2) increasing magnetic field strength ( $I_s \alpha B$ )
(3) using a material having lesser value of torsional constant $\left(I_s \alpha \frac{1}{k}\right)$
(4) increasing area of cross-section of the coil
(Note- Any one of the above )
(b) $R=\frac{V}{I_g}-G$
For range $(0-V)$
$R_1=\frac{V}{I_g}-G$
For range $(0-2 \mathrm{~V})$
$R_2=\frac{2 V}{I_g}-G---$ ....(1)
On solving equations (1) and (2) $\mathrm{G}=\mathrm{R}_2-2 \mathrm{R}_1$....(2)

(a) For a steady current flowing through a uniform wire, the potential difference between any two points is directly proportional to the length of the wire between the two points
(b) Potential gradient $=\frac{5}{1000} \mathrm{Vcm}^{-1}$
$E_1+E_2=700 \times \frac{5}{1000}=3.5 \mathrm{~V}$ (i)
$E_1-E_2=100 \times \frac{5}{1000}=0.5 \mathrm{~V}$ (ii)
Solving these two equations, we get $\mathrm{E}_1=2 \mathrm{~V}$ and $\mathrm{E}_2=1.5 \mathrm{~V}$

questions.q:
A galvanometer is an instrument used to show the direction and strength of the current passing through it. In a galvanometer, a coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque and hence gets deflected when a current passes through it. The name is derived from the surname of Italian scientist L. Galvani, who in 1791 discovered that electric current makes a dead frog's leg jerk. A spring attached with the coil provides a counter torque.
In equilibrium, the deflecting torque is balanced by the restoring torque of the spring and we have :
$\mathrm{NBAI}=\mathbf{k}_\phi$
where N is the total number of turns in the coil
$A$ is the area of cross-section of each turn
$B$ is the radial magnetic field
k is the torsional constant of the spring
$\phi$ is the angular deflection of the coil
As the current ($I_g$) which produces full scale deflection in the galvanometer is very small, the galvanometer cannot as such be used to measure current in electric circuits. A small resistance, called shunt, of a suitable value is connected with the galvanometer to convert it into an ammeter of desired range. By using a higher resistance, a galvanometer can also be converted into a voltmeter.

Question 1
The value of the current sensitivity of a galvanometer is given by:
1. $\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\text { NBA }}$
2. $\frac{\text { NBA }}{\mathrm{k}}$
3. $\frac{\mathrm{kBA}}{\mathrm{N}}$
4. $\frac{\mathrm{kNB}}{\mathrm{A}}$

Question 2
A galvanometer of resistance $6 \Omega$ shows full scale deflection for a current of $0.2 \mathrm{~A}$. The value of shunt to be used with this galvanometer to convert it into an ammeter of range $(0-5 \mathrm{~A})$ is :
1. $0-25 \Omega$
2. $0 \cdot 30 \Omega$
3. $0.50 \Omega$
4. $6 \cdot 0 \Omega$

Question 3
The value of resistance of the ammeter in case (ii) will be :
1. $0 \cdot 20 \Omega$
2. $0 \cdot 24 \Omega$
3. $6 \cdot 0 \Omega$
4. $6 \cdot 25 \Omega$

Question 4
(a) A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter of range $(0-V)$ by connecting with it, a resistance $R_1$. If $R_1$ is replaced by $R_2$, the range becomes $(0-2 \mathrm{~V})$. The resistance of the galvanometer is :
1. $\left(\mathrm{R}_2-2 \mathrm{R}_1\right)$
2. $\left(R_2-R_1\right)$
3. $\left(R_1+R_2\right)$
4. $\left(R_1-2 R_2\right)$

Question 5
(b) A current of 5 mA flows through a galvanometer. Its coil has 100 turns, each of area of cross-section $18 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ and is suspended in a magnetic field 0.20 T. The deflecting torque acting on the coil will be :
1. $3.6 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{Nm}$
2. $1.8 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{Nm}$
3. $2.4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{Nm}$
4. $1 \cdot 2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{Nm}$
questions.solution:
Question 1
Correct Option: $\frac{\text { NBA }}{\mathrm{k}}$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 2
Correct Option: $0.25 \Omega$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 3
Correct Option: $0 \cdot 24 \Omega$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 4
Correct Option: $\left(\mathrm{R}_2-2 \mathrm{R}_1\right)$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 5
Correct Option: $1.8 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{Nm}$
Solution: No Solution.

questions.q:
In a metallic conductor, an electron, moving due to thermal motion, suffers collisions with the heavy fixed ions but after collision, it will emerge out with the same speed but in random directions. If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be zero. When an electric field is applied, electrons move with an average velocity, known as drift velocity $\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}\right)$. The average time between successive collisions is known as relaxation time $(\tau)$. The magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric field is called mobility ($\mu$).
An expression for current through the conductor can be obtained in terms of drift velocity, number of electrons per unit volume (n), electronic charge (-e), and the cross-sectional area (A) of the conductor. This expression leads to an expression between current density $(\hat{j})$ and the electric field $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}})$. Hence, an expression for resistivity $(\rho)$ of a metal is obtained. This expression helps us to understand increase in resistivity of a metal with increase in its temperature, in terms of change in the relaxation time $(\tau)$ and change in the number density of electrons $(\mathrm{n})$.

Question 1
Consider two cylindrical conductors A and B, made of the same metal connected in series to a battery. The length and the radius of $B$ are twice that of $A$. If $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ are the mobility of electrons in $A$ and $B$ respectively, then $\frac{\mu_A}{\mu_B}$ is :
1. $\frac{1}{2}$
2. $\frac{1}{4}$
3. $2$
4. $1$

Question 2
A wire of length 0.5 m and cross-sectional area $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}^2$ is connected to a battery of 2 V that maintains a current of 1.5 A in it. The conductivity of the material of the wire (in $\Omega^{-1} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$ ) is:
1. $2.5 \times 10^4$
2. $3.0 \times 10^5$
3. $3.75 \times 10^6$
4. $5.0 \times 10^7$

Question 3
The temperature coefficient of resistance of nichrome is $1.70 \times 10^{-4}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$. In order to increase resistance of a nichrome wire by $8.5 \%$, the temperature of the wire should be increased by:
1. $250^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
2. $500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
3. $850^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
4. $1000^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

Question 4
(a) Consider the contribution of the following two factors I and II in resistivity of a metal :
I. Relaxation time of electrons
II. Number of electrons per unit volume
The resistivity of a metal increases with increase in its temperature because :
1. I decreases and II increases.
2. I increases and II is almost constant.
3. Both I and II increase.
4. I decreases and II is almost constant.

Question 5
(b) A steady current flows in a copper wire of non-uniform cross-section. Consider the following three physical quantities:
I. Electric field
II. Current density
III. Drift speed
Then at the different points along the wire :
1. II and III change, but I is constant.
2. I and II change, but III is constant.
3. I and III change, but II is constant.
4. All I, II and III change.
questions.solution:
Question 1
Correct Option: $1$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 2
Correct Option: $3.75 \times 10^6$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 3

Solution: No Solution.

Question 4
Correct Option: I decreases and II is almost constant.
Solution: No Solution.

Question 5
Correct Option: All I, II and III change.
Solution: No Solution.

questions.q:
When the terminals of a cell are connected to a conductor of resistance $R$, an electric current flows through the circuit. The electrolyte of the cell also offers some resistance in the path of the current, like the conductor. This resistance offered by the electrolyte is called internal resistance of the cell (r). It depends upon the nature of the electrolyte, the area of the electrodes immersed in the electrolyte and the temperature. Due to internal resistance, a part of the energy supplied by the cell is wasted in the form of heat.
When no current is drawn from the cell, the potential difference between the two electrodes in known as emf of the cell ($\varepsilon$). With a current drawn from the cell, the potential difference between the two electrodes is termed as terminal potential difference (V).

Question 1
Choose the incorrect statement :
1. The potential difference (V) between the two terminals of a cell in a closed circuit is always less than its emf ($\varepsilon$), during discharge of the cell.
2. The internal resistance of a cell decreases with the decrease in temperature of the electrolyte.
3. When current is drawn from the cell then $V=\varepsilon-I r$.
4. The graph between potential difference between the two terminals of the cell (V) and the current (I) through it is a straight line with a negative slope.

Question 2
Two cells of emfs 2.0 V and 6.0 V and internal resistances $0.1 \Omega$ and $0 \cdot 4 \Omega$ respectively, are connected in parallel. The equivalent emf of the combination will be :
1. 2.0 V
2. $2 \cdot 8 \mathrm{~V}$
3. 6.0 V
4. 8.0 V

Question 3
Dipped in the solution, the electrode exchanges charges with the electrolyte. The positive electrode develops a potential $\mathrm{V}_{+}\left(\mathrm{V}_{+}>0\right)$, and the negative electrode develops a potential - $\left(\mathrm{V}_{-}\right)\left(\mathrm{V}_{-} \geq 0\right)$, relative to the electrolyte adjacent to it. When no current is drawn from the cell then :
1. $\varepsilon=V_{+}+V_{-}>0$
2. $\varepsilon=V_{+}-V_{-}>0$
3. $\varepsilon=V_{+}+V_{-}<0$
4. $\varepsilon=V_{+}+V_{-}=0$

Question 4
(a) Five identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance $0.1 \Omega$ are connected in parallel. This combination in turn is connected to an external resistor of $9.98 \Omega$. The current flowing through the resistor is :
1. 0.05 A
2. $0 \cdot 1 \mathrm{~A}$
3. 0.15 A
4. $0 \cdot 2 \mathrm{~A}$

Question 5
(b) Potential difference across a cell in the open circuit is 6 V. It becomes 4 V when a current of 2 A is drawn from it. The internal resistance of the cell is :
1. $1 \cdot 0 \Omega$
2. $1.5 \Omega$
3. $2 \cdot 0 \Omega$
4. $2 \cdot 5 \Omega$
questions.solution:
Question 1
Correct Option: The internal resistance of a cell decreases with the decrease in temperature of the electrolyte.
Solution: No Solution.

Question 2
Correct Option: $2 \cdot 8 \mathrm{~V}$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 3
Correct Option: $\varepsilon=V_{+}+V_{-}>0$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 4
Correct Option: $0 \cdot 2 \mathrm{~A}$
Solution: No Solution.

Question 5
Correct Option: $1 \cdot 0 \Omega$
Solution: No Solution.

questions.q:
(i) Define mobility of electrons. Give its SI units.
(ii) A steady current flows through a wire $A B$, as shown in the figure. What happens to the electric field and the drift velocity along the wire? Justify your answer.

(iii) Consider the circuit shown in the figure. Find the effective resistance of the circuit and the current drawn from the battery.
questions.solution:
(i) Mobility: Mobility is defined as the magnitude of the drift velocity per unit electric field.
$\text { S.I. Unit: } \frac{m^2}{V . s} \text { or } \frac{C . s}{k g}$
(ii) Both electric field and the drift velocity decreases.
Justification:
$v_d=\frac{I}{n e A}$
As area increases across the wire, drift velocity decreases.
$v_d=\frac{e E}{m} \tau$
As drift velocity decreases, electric field decreases (since $\mathrm{e}, \mathrm{m}$ and $\tau$ are constant).
(iii) From the diagram
$10 \Omega$ and $14 \Omega$ are in series $\mathrm{R}_1=10 \Omega+14 \Omega=24 \Omega$
$10 \Omega$ and $10 \Omega$ are in series $\mathrm{R}_2=10 \Omega+10 \Omega=20 \Omega$
$24 \Omega, 20 \Omega$ and $30 \Omega$ are in parallel.
$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{24}+\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{30}=\frac{5+6+4}{120}=\frac{15}{120}$
$\mathrm{R}=8 \Omega$
Electric current in the circuit
$I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{6}{8}=\frac{3}{4} A$
Note: Full credit of $1 \frac{1}{2}$ marks is to be awarded for part (iii) even if a student does not attempt this part.

(a) State the working principle of a meter bridge used to measure an unknown resistance.
(b) Give reason
(i) why the connections between the resistors in a metre bridge are made of thick copper strips,
(ii) why is it generally preferred to obtain the balance length near the mid-point of the bridge wire.
(c) Calculate the potential difference across the $4 \Omega$ resistor in the given electrical circuit, using Kirchhoff's rules.
questions.solution:
(a) Meter bridge is based on the principle of balanced Wheatstone bridge.
(b) (i) Thick copper strips are used to minimize resistance of connections which are not accounted for in the bridge formula
(ii) Balance point is preferred near midpoint of bridge wire to minimize percentage error in resistance (R).
(c)
$I=I_1+I_2$
In loop $A B C D A$
$-8+2 I_1-1 \times I_2+6=0$ ...(2)
In loop $D E F C D$
$-4 I-1 \times I_2+6=0$
$4 I+I_2=6$
$4\left(I_1+I_2\right)+I_2=6$
From equations (1) and (2) we get
$I_1=\frac{8}{7} A, I_2=\frac{2}{7} A, I=\frac{10}{7}$
Potential difference across resistor $4 \Omega$ is:
$V=\frac{10}{7} \times 4=\frac{40}{7} \text { volt }$

questions.q:
(i) State the two Kirchhoff's laws. Explain briefly how these rules are justified.
(ii) The current is drawn from a cell of emf E and internal resistance r connected to the network of resistors each of resistance $r$ as shown in the figure. Obtain the expression for (i) the current draw from the cell and (ii) the power consumed in the network.
questions.solution:
(i) Junction Rule: At any Junction, the sum of currents, entering the junction, is equal to the sum of currents leaving the junction. Loop Rule: The Algebraic sum, of changes in potential, around any closed loop involving resistors and cells, in the loop is zero.
$\sum(\Delta V)=0$
Justification: The first law is in accord with the law of conservation of charge.
The Second law is in accord with the law of conservation of energy.
ii) Equivalent resistance of the loop
$\mathrm{R}=r / 3$
Hence current drawn from the cell
$\mathrm{I}=\frac{E}{r / 3+r}=\frac{3 E}{4 r}$
Power consumed $\mathrm{P}=I^2(r / 3)$
$=\frac{9 E^2}{16 r^2} \times 4 r / 3=\frac{3 E^2}{4 r}$
[Note: Award the last $11 / 2$ marks for this part, if the calculations, for these parts, are done by using (any other) value of equivalent resistance obtained by the student.)

questions.q:
(i) Define the term drift velocity.
(ii) On the basis of electron drift, derive an expression for resistivity of a conductor in terms of number density of free electrons and relaxation time. On what factors does resistivity of a conductor depend?
(iii) Why alloys like constantan and manganin are used for making standard resistors ?
questions.solution:
i) Average velocity acquired by the electrons in the conductor in the presence of external electric field.
[Alternatively:
$v_d=\frac{-e E \tau}{m}$ where $\tau$ is the relaxation time.]
ii) $v_d=\frac{-e E \tau}{m}$
We have $E=-\frac{V}{\ell}$, where $V$ is potential difference across the length ' $\ell$ ' of the conductor
$v_d=\frac{e V \tau}{m \ell}$
Current flowing $I=n e A v_d$
$I=n e A v_d \frac{e V \tau}{m \ell}=\frac{n e^2 A V \tau}{m \ell}$
$\frac{I}{V}=\frac{n e^2 A \tau}{m \ell}=\frac{1}{R}$ .....(i)
Also, $\mathrm{R}=\rho \frac{\ell}{A}$ ...(ii)
Comparing (i) and (ii)
$\rho=\frac{m}{n e^2 \tau}$
Resistivity of the material of a conductor depends on the relaxation time, i.e., temperature and the number density of electrons.
iii) Because constantan and manganin show very weak dependence of resistivity on temperature
